heading_path: Financial assistance
text:
At Penn Medicine, we offer patients financial counseling and assistance to those who need it.

Do you have a Medicaid plan? New federal Medicaid rules are coming on Jan. 1, 2027. The new rules affect how often people with Medicaid need to renew their coverage and what information they need to provide to stay covered.

Learn more

We are committed to caring for all patients equitably, with dignity, respect and compassion without regard to age, race, color, national origin, religious creed, sex, physical or mental disability, marital status or sexual preference.

heading_path: Financial assistance > Caring for all
text:
As part of this commitment, we offer financial counseling and assistance programs to uninsured and underinsured patients to assist those who cannot pay for all or part of their care.

Patients will be considered for financial assistance individually, considering total household income and other resources. Penn Medicine will also consider other factors in the patient/family financial situation, should there be other critical expenses, not related to the patient’s medical care, that make payment of the financial obligation impossible, such as caring for a disabled family member.

Uninsured or underinsured persons may apply for financial assistance at any time during treatment here or when request for payment is made.

heading_path: Financial assistance > Request financial assistance

source_title: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills
heading_path: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills > The No Surprises Act
text:
The No Surprises Act protects you from surprise billing and requires us to provide you with a better understanding of your potential out of network financial responsibility.

**The No Surprises Act**

Penn Medicine values patient education, choices in healthcare and financial transparency. We understand the importance of directing patients to the best care for them. For “out of network” patients, there is the potential that getting care from our system could cost more than if that care was obtained from a provider within your insurance’s network.

As of 2022, federal law now protects you from surprise billing and requires us to provide you with a better understanding of your potential out of network financial responsibility:

- When you get emergency care from “out-of-network” providers and facilities, or

- When an “out-of-network” provider treats you at an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center without your knowledge or consent.

Please ask your health care provider or patient financial advocate if you need help understanding if/how these protections apply to you and your out of network plan. When a patient is “out of network” to Penn Medicine, we will work to inform our patients of the potential for increased out of pocket expenses, provide an estimate of services and obtain your consent to agree to pay more for “out of network” care.

Prior to your service, you should contact your health plan to better understand what provider options are available as well as plan to connect with Penn Medicine to review your estimate and consent.

For any questions or concerns regarding the best options for out-of-network care and financial liability, please reach out to [PriceTransparency@uphs.upenn.edu](mailto:PriceTransparency@uphs.upenn.edu) or leave a voicemail on our Financial Advocacy line at [215-662-3505](tel:+1-215-662-3505). Please allow 2 business days for a response.

For more information on the No Surprises Act please see below:

Effective: January 1, 2022

heading_path: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills > The No Surprises Act > Your Rights and Protections Against Surprise Medical Bills
text: When you get emergency care or get treated by an out-of-network provider at an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center, you are protected from balance billing (sometimes called surprise billing).

source_title: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills
heading_path: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills > The No Surprises Act > What is “balance billing” (sometimes called “surprise billing”)?
text:
When you see a doctor or other healthcare provider, you may owe certain out-of-pocket costs, such as a copayment, coinsurance, and/or a deductible. You may have other costs or have to pay the entire bill if you see a provider or visit a healthcare facility that isn’t in your health plan’s network.

“Out-of-network” describes providers and facilities that haven’t signed a contract with your health plan. Out-of-network providers may be permitted to bill you for the difference between what your plan agreed to pay and the full amount charged for a service. This is called “balance billing.” This amount is likely more than in-network costs for the same service and might not count toward your annual out-of-pocket limit.

“Surprise billing” is an unexpected balance bill. This can happen when you can’t control who is involved in your care — like when you have an emergency or when you schedule a visit at an in- network facility but are unexpectedly treated by an out-of-network provider.

source_title: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills
heading_path: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills > The No Surprises Act > You are protected from balance billing for:
text:
Emergency services

If you have an emergency medical condition and get emergency services from an out-of- network provider or facility, the most the provider or facility may bill you is your plan’s in- network cost-sharing amount (such as copayments and coinsurance). You can’t be balance billed for these emergency services. This includes services you may get after you’re in stable condition, unless you give written consent and give up your protections not to be balance billed for these post-stabilization services.

New Jersey law also protects you from being billed for out-of-network services provided on an emergency or urgent basis in an amount in excess of your in-network cost-sharing amount (i.e., the amount your deductible, copayments, or coinsurance would have been if the same services were provided on an in-network basis).

Certain services at an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center

When you get services from an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center, certain providers may be out-of-network. In these cases, the most those providers may bill you is your plan’s in-network cost-sharing amount. This applies to emergency medicine, anesthesia, pathology, radiology, laboratory, neonatology, assistant surgeon, hospitalist or intensivist services. These providers can’t balance bill you and may not ask you to give up your protections not to be balance billed.

If you get other services at these in-network facilities, out-of-network providers can’t balance bill you, unless you give written consent and give up your protections.

You’re never required to give up your protections from balance billing. You also aren’t required to get care out-of-network. You can choose a provider or facility in your plan’s network.

New Jersey law also protects you from being billed for inadvertent out-of-network services (services at an in-network facility provided by out-of-network providers) in an amount in excess of your in-network cost-sharing amount (i.e., the amount your deductible, copayments, or coinsurance would have been if the same services were provided on an in-network basis).

source_title: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills
heading_path: Rights and protections against surprise medical bills > The No Surprises Act > When balance billing isn’t allowed, you also have the following protections:
text:
You are only responsible for paying your share of the cost (like the copayments, coinsurance and deductibles that you would pay if the provider or facility was in-network). Your health plan will pay out-of-network providers and facilities directly.

Your health plan generally must:

- Cover emergency services without requiring you to get approval for services in advance (prior authorization).

- Cover emergency services by out-of-network providers.

- Base what you owe the provider or facility (cost-sharing) on what it would pay an in-network provider or facility and show that amount in your explanation of benefits.

- Count any amount you pay for emergency services or out-of-network services toward your deductible and out-of-pocket limit.

If you have received a larger than expected bill please call billing customer service at [800-406-1177](tel:+1-800-406-1177).

If you believe you’ve been wrongly billed, you may contact the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Department of Health and Human Services at [800-985-3059](tel:+1-800-985-3059).

For services rendered in New Jersey, you also may contact the New Jersey Department of Banking and Insurance at [609-292-7272](tel:+1-609-292-7272) or file an online complaint at: [https://www.state.nj.us/dobi/consumer.htm](https://www.state.nj.us/dobi/consumer.htm).

For more information about your rights under federal law, visit: [https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/consumers](https://www.cms.gov/nosurprises/consumers).

For more information about your rights under New Jersey law, visit: [https://www.state.nj.us/dobi/index.html](https://www.state.nj.us/dobi/index.html).

text:
Penn Medicine’s language assistance provides medical interpreter services for all patients, family members and visitors.

Penn Medicine’s medical interpreter services are provided through professional medical staff interpreters, phone interpretation, video remote interpretation, and contracted services with interpretation agencies.

heading_path: Language assistance > Frequently asked questions about language services and interpretation > Can a family member or friend interpret for me?
text: We encourage you to bring your family members with you and have them involved in decisions concerning your care. However, Lancaster General Health has a policy regarding communication with limited English proficiency patients and deaf and hard of hearing patients. LG Health must use only qualified interpreters.

heading_path: Language assistance > Frequently asked questions about language services and interpretation > How can I request an interpreter if I am hospitalized?
text:
**How can I request an interpreter for future appointments?**

If you are scheduling appointments for tests or procedures, ask the scheduler to request an interpreter for your appointment. Please state your language preference.

**How can I request an interpreter if I am hospitalized?**

Please contact your nurse, who will arrange interpretation services during your stay. If the patient is unable to make a request, a family member may contact the nurse to arrange interpretation services on his or her behalf.

heading_path: Language assistance > Frequently asked questions about language services and interpretation > What interpretation services are available for deaf or hard of hearing patients?
text: For patients, family members or visitors who are Deaf or Hard of Hearing, and who communicate primarily in ASL the organization provides Video Remote Interpreting (VRI) services in ASL, and/or contracted agency ASL interpreters.

heading_path: Language assistance > Frequently asked questions about language services and interpretation > Who will interpret for me?
text:
**What is Video Remote Interpretation (VRI)?**

Video Remote Interpretation or VRI uses video technology to provide interpreting services through a qualified remote interpreter who is not present in the same room as the other parties.

**Who will interpret for me?**

A member of our team of professional medical Spanish interpreters can help facilitate effective communication between you and your health care provider. We also have qualified bilingual personnel trained as medical interpreters to assist staff members with patients who need interpretation services in other languages. All our staff interpreters wear an orange badge, which will help you to identify them as qualified interpreters, and the language they speak.

heading_path: Language assistance > Frequently asked questions about language services and interpretation > Will I always have an in-person interpreter?
text: Although we try our best to fulfill requests with an interpreter, it is not always possible due to external factors such as language, last minute requests, patients not showing up for pre-scheduled appointments, etc. Our staff will, after assessing patient’s communication needs, use our phone line that provides interpretation services in more than 150 different languages, and VRI services in several languages, including ASL and Spanish. Both services are available 24 hrs. 7 days a week.

heading_path: Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP) > Enrollment of Dependents
text:
Penn students utilizing the Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP) may enroll their lawful spouse/domestic partner and unmarried dependent children under age 26 who reside with, and are fully supported by, the covered student for the same coverage. Student must be enrolled in PSIP before they can enroll spouses or dependents.

Dependent enrollment is processed online at [www.aetnastudenthealth.com/upenn](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://www.aetnastudenthealth.com/en/upenn/index.html__;!!IBzWLUs!VNBy5dFfO-Q0s_tWNLrDbdYXAB78gfxTmvzBeo76GzE9jBXCVRHtIXSbJUKjnZW9g6UvhbPB94piVipZrN-0euE$). All spouses and domestic partners must have a Penn Guest Card to determine dependent status. Students will need to submit a Dependent Enrollment Application with payment directly to Aetna. Contact Aetna at [(800) 841-5374](tel:(800) 841-5374) with any questions regarding dependent enrollment. Dependent premiums may be paid in full or in monthly installments.

- Fall semester deadline: August 31

- Spring semester deadline: January 31

- Summer semester deadline: May 31

The Dependent Enrollment Application and premium will not be accepted after the deadline unless there is a qualifying life event, including the following:

- involuntary loss of health insurance

- marriage

- entry into the US

A certificate of credible coverage stating the date of the involuntary loss of health coverage, marriage certificate or stamped passport along with a signed application must be submitted to Aetna Student Health within 31 days of the qualifying life event. After the 31 days, the dependent would no longer eligible for enrollment in the current policy year.

heading_path: Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP) > Newborn Infant and Adopted Child Coverage
text:
A child born to a Covered Person shall be covered for Preventative Care, Accident, Sickness, and congenital defects, for 31 days from the date of birth. At the end of this 31 day period, coverage will cease under the University of Pennsylvania Student Health Insurance Plan. To extend coverage for a newborn past the 31 days, the covered student must:

1. Enroll the child within 31 days of birth, AND

2. Pay the additional premium, starting from the date of birth

Coverage is provided for a child legally placed for adoption with a covered student for 31 days from the moment of placement provided the child lives in the household of the covered student, and is dependent upon the covered student for support. To extend coverage for an adopted child past the 31 days, the covered student must:

1. Enroll the child within 31 days of placement of such child, AND

2. Pay any additional premium, if necessary, starting from the date of placement.

For information or general questions on dependent enrollment, contact Aetna Student Health at [(800) 841-5374](tel:(800) 841-5374).

heading_path: Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP) > Dental Coverage for Students
text:

heading_path: Insurance Navigation > 2026-2027 Academic Year > What is the University’s insurance criteria?
text:
Students in the Philadelphia area must have insurance that meets the following standards. If you are covered under your own health insurance or that of your parents, you may maintain your coverage if it meets the following criteria:

- Your insurance plan must be provided by a company licensed to do business in the United States, with a U.S. claims payment office and a U.S. telephone number. The company must have a process to remit payments to providers within the U.S.

- Your insurance plan must provide coverage for pre-existing conditions, or have been in effect long enough that any waiting period has passed.

- Your insurance plan must offer an annual maximum benefit of at least $2,000,000.

- Your insurance plan must provide for both in-patient and out-patient mental health care in the Philadelphia area. A policy that provides only emergency or urgent mental health care services in this area does not meet this requirement. *

- Your insurance plan must provide coverage for both in-patient and out-patient medical care in the Philadelphia area, including routine office visits, specialist office visits, diagnostic testing, imaging and physical therapy. A policy that provides only emergency or urgent medical care in this area does not meet this requirement.*

*If you are insured with an out-of-area managed care plan (i.e. HMO or similar plan), you should be aware that most managed care plans do not cover any care outside of the plan network other than urgent and emergency services. Unless your insurance carrier provides you with a rider for out-of-area coverage in the Philadelphia area, your waiver will not be approved.

heading_path: Insurance Navigation > 2026-2027 Academic Year > What do I need to know before I enroll into or waive out of the Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP)?
text:
Students must enroll into or waive out of the Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP) every year. If you waive out of PSIP, you will be asked to submit your health insurance for verification that it meets the University requirements.

You will need to have a PennKey and password to access the Penn Student Insurance Portal. The PennKey is your link to most of the electronic resources that you will need while here on campus. If you are a first year student, contact your school to find out how to obtain a PennKey (or visit the [PennKey website](https://pennkeysupport.upenn.edu/help-for-students).)

IMPORTANT: If you receive a message stating that you don’t have access to this site, this may be because we have not yet received your registration information from the University. Please try back in few days. If the problem persists longer than a week, please contact the Insurance Navigators at [215-746-4200](tel:215-746-4200) or email us at [wel-shsinsur@pobox.upenn.edu](mailto:wel-shsinsur@pobox.upenn.edu).

If your health insurance changes at any point during the academic year, your coverage must be updated in person in the Immunization and Insurance Compliance Office. You cannot change the date of enrollment. Once you have completed your selection, you will receive a confirmation email. You can also visit the Insurance Portal again to view your selection information and the status of your waiver request.

If you are a student enrolling in the Penn Student Insurance Plan, please be aware that you will also be charged the Clinical Fee in order to access Student Health and Counseling as your primary care provider.

The Insurance Portal opens and closes at various points throughout the year:

heading_path: Insurance Navigation > 2026-2027 Academic Year > What are the referral requirements?
text:
Students covered under the Penn Student Insurance Plan should first seek medical treatment at Student Health and Counseling for each medical condition if within 25 miles of Student Health and Counseling. The Student Health and Counseling provider will refer you, if appropriate, to an outside provider in advance of your appointment. A new referral for each condition is required at the beginning of each policy year.

Any care received within 25 miles of Student Health and Counseling without a prior Student Health and Counseling referral will be payable subject to the Non-Preferred Benefit, including the $1,500 Deductible.

A referral is not required in the following circumstances:

- Treatment for an emergency medical condition

- The student is more than 25 miles away from Student Health and Counseling

- Annual eye exams, services, and supplies

- Injury to sound natural teeth or removal of impacted wisdom teeth

- Preventive or routine services

- Reproductive health and voluntary termination of pregnancy

- Inpatient and outpatient mental health and substance use services

- Pediatric care

- Students on leave of absence

- Outpatient lab services

- Care for dependents

The referral requirement does not apply to covered dependents or when Student Health and Counseling is closed. Referrals expire July 31. Please contact Student Health and Counseling for all questions about referrals.

heading_path: Appointments > Instructions for NEW PATIENTS to schedule your online appointment:
text:
**24/7 Support**

Call [215-746-WELL](tel:215-746-WELL) (9355) or schedule your medical care appointment online through your [PennChart account](https://secure.mypennmedicine.org/MyPennMedicine/Authentication/Login?).

**Instructions for NEW PATIENTS to schedule your online appointment:**

1. Download the MyChart app in the App Store or Google Play or visit the [PennChart website](https://secure.mypennmedicine.org/MyPennMedicine/Authentication/Login?).

2. Log into (or create) your myPennMedicine account.

3. Once logged in, click on “Schedule an Appointment” and then select “All Options.”

4. From there, you must select "Primary Care" no matter what your medical concern is.

5. On the next screen, you must choose your visit type by selecting "UPenn Student Wellness Visit - Primary Care." Then select "Student."

6. Enter your Penn ID and answer the question about urgent symptoms. After that, choose your appointment type by selecting the option that best matches the reason for your visit:

  - Gynecological: contraception evaluation, menstrual problems, PCOS/PMOS, and more

  - Injury: joint pain, recent injuries, and more

  - Routine Care: physicals, nutrition, asymptomatic STI testing, gender-affirming care, PrEP, and more

  - Sick Visit: non-chronic illness symptoms

7. Find the appointment that best fits your schedule.

8. Follow the prompts to finalize and be sure to arrive on time for your appointment.

Please note: if the visit type you need cannot be scheduled online, a pop-up will appear directing you to call the Medical Care office at 215-746-WELL (9355).

heading_path: Immunization Navigation > 2026-2027 Academic Year > Wellness at Penn: Statement about the University’s Immunization Requirements
text:
Penn’s vaccination policy is informed by requirements from the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania as well as established scientific evidence demonstrating that immunizations are effective in preventing outbreaks and protecting the health and wellbeing of the campus population and its surrounding communities. These measures are especially important for safeguarding individuals who are under-vaccinated, unable to receive vaccines, or immunocompromised.

In alignment with the [Governor’s Executive Order 2025-02](https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/governor/documents/Executive%20Order%202025%2002%20Governor%20Shapiro%20Vaccines%20Access.pdf), Penn continues to rely on guidance from leading medical and public health authorities including, but not limited to, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), as well as the American College Health Association (ACHA). Our clinicians use this evidence-based guidance to support student health and promote a safe and healthy learning environment.

Penn remains committed to science-based public health practices and to fostering a campus environment in which all students can thrive.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > I can’t find my immunization records; do I need to have my shots again?
text:
**What immunizations are required?**

You can find the list of required immunizations here on the [Immunization Requirements](https://wellness.upenn.edu/immunization-insurance-compliance/immunization-compliance) page.

**I can’t find my immunization records; do I need to have my shots again?**

If you aren't able to locate your immunization records, you must see a physician so that they can perform a test that will check your blood for antibodies. They can then enter this information on the Student Immunization Record. You can have these tests done at [Student Health and Counseling](https://wellness.upenn.edu/student-health-and-counseling) at your own expense, unless it is covered by your health insurance.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > How much do my immunizations cost?
text: Students with the Penn Student Insurance Plan (PSIP) are fully covered for required immunizations. In addition, the Affordable Care Act mandates that essential benefits, including certain immunizations and vaccines, be covered with no cost sharing. Please check with your health insurance carrier to see what vaccines are covered and how you can be reimbursed in the event that you obtain the immunizations at Student Health and Counseling. Learn more about vaccine costs here: [Wellness Vaccine and Titer Prices](https://upenn.box.com/s/dut3nitgx6nbr20fip3af5yreonv62np).

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > I made a mistake on my online form, what should I do?
text: You should alert our Immunization and Insurance Navigators that the information you submitted is different than the information on your documentation. Your healthcare provider’s documentation is the document of record.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What happens if I don't upload my immunization forms?
text: Failure to comply with the University’s immunization requirements and to submit the Student Immunization Record and/or the Student Medical History and Consent form will result in having a hold placed on your registration, which will make you unable to register and attend certain classes. If you do not have any online immunization information to enter, please alert the immunization office.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > I’m on registration hold. What do I do now?
text: First, check your messages in PennChart as there are likely instructions for next steps there. If there are not, contact our Immunization and Insurance Navigators. We can then explain why you are on hold and what you will need to do. Only the Immunization and Insurance Navigators can remove your hold. Because this involves your protected health information, we will NOT discuss this with third parties such as your school administration, professors, parents, or anyone else without your explicit consent.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > If I become compliant will I be taken off hold automatically?
text: No. The process is not automatic; it typically takes about 24 hours for a hold to be removed once you have become compliant. Please contact our Immunization and Insurance Navigators at 215-746-4200. Holds can only be removed during regular office hours.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > Do graduate students living off campus need to submit the immunization form AND documentation?
text:
Non-healthcare graduate students living off campus can submit the immunization form OR documentation from a provider/previous University.

Healthcare graduate students must submit their immunization form AND documentation from a provider/previous University.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What is Penn’s TB testing requirement?
text:
All full-time Penn students must complete an online TB risk factor screening questionnaire. Only those students who are considered to be in a high risk group for TB infection will need to be tested. Our Immunization and Insurance Navigators will contact you if you need to be tested for TB.

Healthcare students are required to submit a two-step PPD. The first step can be accepted from a US provider in last 12 months. The second step must be completed at Student Health and Counseling. IGRA blood test (Quantiferon TB Gold or T-Spot-TB) taken within last six months can take place of the two-step PPD.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What are the options for TB testing?
text: Students whose TB screening questionnaire indicates that they need testing can either get a tuberculin skin test (also known as PPD) at Student Health and Counseling after they arrive on campus or they can get a TB blood test, such as the Quantiferon Gold or TSpotTB. Please note that Penn does not accept PPD tests that are administered outside of Student Health and Counseling. However, Penn does accept TB blood tests from outside healthcare providers that were performed within the past year (or within six months of entrance into Penn).

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What if I have had a positive test for TB infection in the past?
text: Students with a history of latent or active TB must schedule an appointment at Student Health and Counseling, and provide documentation of positive PPD skin test or IGRA blood test. Students must also submit a copy of their negative radiology report (chest x-ray performed in the US). International chest x-rays are not accepted. Films and CDs are not accepted. TB symptom checks are required annually.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > Do I have to be immunized against meningitis?
text: All incoming students who will be living in campus housing and who are age 21 or younger must submit proof of one dose on or after age 16 of meningococcal conjugate vaccine that covers serogroups A, C, Y, and W-135. Incoming students living on campus who are over age 21 should submit proof of vaccination on or after age 16 or request an exemption. If you are seeking an exemption, please email [wel-immun@pobox.upenn.edu](mailto:wel-immun@pobox.upenn.edu) and identify whether it is a medical or religious exemption request for meningococcal vaccine.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > I’m told that I can’t have the third hepatitis B vaccine for several months after the 2nd dose. What do I do?
text:
**I live off campus. Do I have to have meningococcal immunization or submit a waiver?**

No, you do not need to submit the waiver. Meningococcal vaccine is still recommended, but is not required, for students living off campus.

**I’m told that I can’t have the third hepatitis B vaccine for several months after the 2nd dose. What do I do?**

We don’t require the third vaccine until your second semester. We will give you the proper time to finish the vaccine series.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > Does proof a Td vaccine satisfy the requirement for a Tdap vaccine?
text: No. The University of Pennsylvania requires a dose of Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis) within the past 10 years. Why? Guidance from the Philadelphia Department of Public Health and the American College Health Association recommend Tdap to help prevent outbreaks of pertussis on our campus. Pertussis immunity wains quickly, so the Tdap, instead of just a TD booster, offers the best protection in support of the health of our campus.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What if I have a negative Hepatitis B titer after 2 full series?
text: Healthcare students who have a negative Hepatitis B titer after two full series must submit two completed three-dose series AND submit two negative titers AND schedule a primary care appointment with Student Health and Counseling upon arrival to campus.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What if I have a history of Hepatitis illness?
text: Healthcare students who have a history of Hepatitis illness must submit medical documentation and bloodwork reports AND schedule a primary care appointment with Student Health and Counseling upon arrival to campus.

heading_path: FAQs: Immunization Requirements > What if I have more questions?
text: You can call our Immunization and Insurance Navigators at 215-746-4200.

heading_path: Individual Therapy
text: Student Health and Counseling offers solution-oriented, short-term care that is tailored to fit each student’s unique needs. Our services are free and confidential, and may be offered in-person and virtually in some circumstances. Nothing is too big or too small. Please remember, we are always available for urgent needs.

heading_path: Individual Therapy > Let's Talk and Drop-In Services
text:
Let’s Talk

Let’s Talk provides access to free and confidential drop-in conversations with a trained professional at various locations across campus. Students can talk about any stress and anxiety they are feeling, bounce around ideas, and work through their emotions.

Some common concerns might include:

- Stress

- Sadness

- Difficulty adjusting to school

- Academic concerns

- Concentration and attention difficulty

- Family & financial problems

- Relationship concerns

[Learn More About Let's Talk](https://wellness.upenn.edu/counseling/lets-talk)

Drop-In Services

Students can drop-in to the Student Health and Counseling office (3624 Market Street) at any time during regular business hours for counseling support.

heading_path: Individual Therapy > Psychiatric Medication Management
text:
Our psychiatry team includes psychiatric nurse practitioners and psychiatrists who provide psychiatric evaluations, medication management, and case management to students in concurrent counseling who are seeking those services. Students can receive a referral for a psychiatric evaluation from their counselor. Since most psychological and emotional concerns are best addressed by counseling, psychiatry team members work in collaboration with their counseling colleagues to provide the most effective overall care for each student.

The following are important considerations before a student starts a psychotropic medication:

- If a student is wanting to start a medication near the end of the semester and is planning on leaving the Philadelphia area, it may not be possible for our psychiatry team members to start that medication. If the student leaves the area, the prescriber would not be able to provide the appropriate medical follow-up necessary to ensure the medication is working in a safe and effective manner. Initial prescriptions will likely not be written during and after the last two weeks of classes, however, students can be connected with our referral services to find care at their future location.

- If a student is already on medications prescribed by a member of our psychiatry team and is planning to be away for the summer or on a semester studying abroad, our team may continue to prescribe for the student depending on the stability of the student and the need for follow-up. Students will need to speak with their current prescriber about their care away from Philadelphia.

- Students must inform our psychiatry team members about their substance use before being prescribed medication. Substance use includes the regular use of alcohol, cannabis, vaping any substance, and the use of any illicit or controlled substance. Failure to disclose this information can result in serious consequences to the student’s health.

ADHD Care Navigation

If a student is seeking to establish or continue treatment for [Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)](https://www.cdc.gov/adhd/index.html), they should visit our [ADHD Care Navigation](https://wellness.upenn.edu/adhd) page. Academic accommodations are processed through the [Weingarten Center](https://wlrc.vpul.upenn.edu/), located at Hamilton Village (220 South 40th Street, Suite 260). They can be reached at [215-573-9235](tel:215-573-9235).

heading_path: Individual Therapy > Referral and Consultation Services
text:

Referrals are also used for students who are interested in psychoeducational testing, couples counseling and/or higher levels of care. Students may also seek referrals for a specific counseling approach or when seeking a provider of a specific identity or background. Students make the final decision about whether or not they can work with a particular outside provider.

heading_path: Individual Therapy > Sexual Trauma Treatment Outreach and Prevention (STTOP)
text:
The Sexual Trauma Treatment Outreach and Prevention (STTOP) Team is a multidisciplinary team of clinicians dedicated to providing confidential care, support, and advocacy to students who have experienced sexual trauma during their academic career. The culture of silence surrounding sexual assault and rape on campus and within our culture as a whole deters reporting, isolates victim-survivors, and undermines the safety and public health of all members of a community. The STTOP Team is committed to providing immediate support to students in need and to promoting awareness and change through active participation in campus outreach and collaboration with community partners.

Confidentiality

Student Health and Counseling offers confidential and free professional services to undergraduate, graduate and professional students at Penn. Students should call our team at [215-746-WELL](tel:215-746-WELL) (9355) and select option 1 to speak with a mental health professional 24/7 or select option 2 to reach the front desk who can help schedule an appointment with a STTOP clinician. Students will be asked routine questions; it is their decision what details they feel comfortable disclosing. It is up to them whether they want to name or identify the offender. Students do not have to tell family members, academic programs, or law enforcement, and they do not have to file a report with the university in order to receive care.

Penn Violence Prevention

Penn Violence Prevention is a collaborative program which works to engage the Penn community in the prevention of sexual violence, relationship violence, and stalking on campus. For more information about resources on campus, reporting options, or how to support a friend, visit the [Penn Violence Prevention](https://pvp.universitylife.upenn.edu/) website.

Contact the STTOP Team Virtually

Students who have experienced rape, sexual assault, stalking or an unsafe or confusing sexual encounter should call our team at [215-746-WELL](tel:215-746-WELL) (9355) to speak with a mental health professional 24/7.

Sexual Assault/Trauma Workshops

We offer a variety of workshops that center around conversations on intimacy, boundaries, safety, and trauma within relationships. Examples of topics include communicating consent, healthy/positive sexuality, and healthy relationships. We also provide safe spaces for individuals who identify as survivors to come together, find community, and cultivate pathways towards healing. Additionally, based on the principles of trauma-informed care, we offer workshops to support providers and caregivers on the impact of trauma on victim/survivor’s health and wellness.

Frequently Asked Questions

heading_path: Individual Therapy > Sexual Trauma Treatment Outreach and Prevention (STTOP)
text:
- Was what happened to me bad enough to count?  If you experienced an unsafe or confusing sexual encounter or relationship and you are considering reaching out to the STTOP team, we encourage you to do so. You do not need to put a label on your experience to receive help. You are entitled to respect and whatever support you need.

- Where can I find information on healthy sexuality?  It can be difficult to find information on healthy sexuality and sex positive behaviors. For more information on healthy sexuality including resources, glossaries, and scenarios for discussion, see the [National Sexual Violence Resource Center](https://www.nsvrc.org/find-help). Students are encouraged to sign up for [Vibe](https://wellness.upenn.edu/vibe), Wellness at Penn's digital sex education program.

- Where can I find other resources on campus?  For more information about resources, please visit our [Get Help Now](https://wellness.upenn.edu/get-help-now) page. You can also reach out to [Penn Violence Prevention](https://pvp.universitylife.upenn.edu/), [Special Services](https://www.publicsafety.upenn.edu/about/special-services/), the [Women’s Center](https://pwc.vpul.upenn.edu/), and [Student Health and Counseling](https://wellness.upenn.edu/student-health-and-counseling). We encourage students to reach out to whichever resource they feel most comfortable with.

- How can I support my friend?  Supporting a friend who has been assaulted, stalked or abused can be really hard. The role friends play in supporting survivors is essential, and it’s different from that of a counselor, lawyer, or doctor. For information about helping a friend, please visit the [Penn Violence Prevention](https://pvp.universitylife.upenn.edu/) website.

heading_path: Individual Therapy > LGBTQ+ Care
text:
Wellness at Penn proudly supports our LGBTQ+ community with dedicated care that helps students feel seen, valued, and empowered. Whether they're exploring identity, navigating relationships, or forging their own path, our affirming therapists are here to listen, understand, and walk alongside them. Through the work of our LGBTQ+ Working Group, we collaborate with students, staff, and campus partners to ensure our services remain inclusive, responsive, and reflective of what our students need.

Our team offers one-on-one assessments and letters that meet professional standards and help support students considering or undergoing gender-affirming care. From exploring options to taking action, we’re here to support our students with clarity, compassion, and respect.

Learn more about our [LGBTQ+ Care](https://wellness.upenn.edu/medical-care/lgbtq-care).

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: I feel sick. Where should I go first?
Answer: Student Health, Medical Care, 3535 Market St, Suite 100. Call 215-746-WELL (9355) to book. True emergency: 911, or PennComm 215-573-3333 on campus.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Do I have to go to Student Health first?
Answer: Yes, for most non-emergency care if you are within 25 miles of campus. Without a Student Health referral, care is paid at the Non-Preferred level with a $1,500 deductible.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Student Health is closed. Where do I go?
Answer: Call 215-746-WELL (9355); a provider is on call 24/7 and will tell you where to go. No referral is needed when Student Health is closed.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: It's Saturday night and I have a high fever. What should I do?
Answer: Call 215-746-WELL (9355) for the on-call provider. If it feels like an emergency, call 911. The bot does not judge how serious it is.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Should I go to urgent care or the ER?
Answer: Urgent care for problems that can't wait but aren't life-threatening; ER for true emergencies, not mild illness. If unsure, call the on-call provider at 215-746-WELL.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Which urgent care near campus takes PSIP?
Answer: Penn lists examples (not endorsements): Vybe Urgent Care Center City, Jefferson Urgent Care at Rittenhouse, Jefferson Urgent Care at Washington Square. Check Aetna's provider search for network status.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Which hospital near campus should I go to in an emergency?
Answer: Penn Medicine ERs: HUP (1 Convention Ave), Penn Presbyterian (51 N. 39th St), Pennsylvania Hospital (800 Spruce St). In an emergency, the nearest ER.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: I need a dentist. Where do I go?
Answer: PSIP covers only injury to natural teeth and impacted wisdom teeth. For routine dental care, buy the Penn Student Dental Plan or the Aetna Student Dental Plan.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: I need an eye exam or glasses. Where do I go?
Answer: Annual eye exams need no referral. Adult eye exam: plan pays 90% in network, 60% out of network, no deductible, 1 exam per year. Glasses or contacts: plan pays 100% up to $125 per year; contact lens fitting visits are not covered. Optional Aetna Vision Preferred plan ($65 per year): exam $10 copay, $130 frame allowance.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: I want to see a therapist. Where do I start?
Answer: Counseling at 3624 Market St, First Floor West. Drop in during hours or call 215-746-WELL (9355) any time. Outside mental health care needs no referral.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: How do I see a specialist?
Answer: Book a Student Health visit first; the provider sends a referral before your specialist appointment.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Can I see a doctor online?
Answer: Yes. Telemedicine visits are covered the same as in-person visits: $35 copay for a doctor or specialist, $10 copay for mental health. The PDFs do not name a specific Aetna 24/7 virtual care service.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Where to go
text:
Question: Is there a nurse I can call for advice?
Answer: Yes: 215-746-WELL (9355), 24/7, connects to Student Health's on-call provider.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: Do I need a referral to see a specialist?
Answer: Yes, if you are within 25 miles of Student Health and none of the exceptions apply.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: How do I get a referral from Student Health?
Answer: See a Student Health provider; they send the referral to the outside provider before your appointment.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: How long is a referral valid?
Answer: Until July 31, the end of the plan year.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: Do I need a new referral for a follow-up visit?
Answer: Not in the same plan year for the same condition. A new referral is needed for each condition each plan year.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: Do I need a referral for urgent care or the ER?
Answer: Not for an emergency, not when Student Health is closed, and not more than 25 miles away. Urgent care while Student Health is open and you are within 25 miles: yes. Urgent care is not a referral exception, so without one the visit is paid at the out-of-network level (plan pays 70% after the $1,500 deductible).

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: Do I need a referral for mental health care?
Answer: No. Inpatient and outpatient mental health and substance use care are exempt.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: I'm more than 25 miles from campus. Do I still need a referral?
Answer: No.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Referrals
text:
Question: What happens if I see a doctor without a referral?
Answer: The claim is paid at the Non-Preferred level, with a $1,500 deductible, so you pay much more.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: Is a Student Health visit free?
Answer: Visits are covered by the Clinical Fee ($385 per semester), which all full-time students pay. Some items, like labs sent to an outside lab, are billed to insurance.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: Will my blood test cost money?
Answer: It may. Labs sent to an outside lab are billed to your insurance. Outpatient labs need no referral. At an in-network lab you pay a $35 copay; at an out-of-network lab the plan pays 70% after the deductible.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: How much is an urgent care visit with PSIP?
Answer: $35 copay in network, no further cost. Out of network: plan pays 70% after the deductible. Non-urgent use of urgent care is not covered.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: How much is an ER visit with PSIP?
Answer: $100 copay per visit, no deductible. Out-of-network ERs are paid the same as in network. The copay is waived if you are admitted. Non-emergency use of the ER is not covered. No referral needed for emergencies.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: How much does a specialist visit cost?
Answer: With referral: $35 copay per visit. Without referral: paid at the out-of-network level (plan pays 70% after the $1,500 deductible).

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: How much will an X-ray or MRI cost?
Answer: X-ray and lab work: $35 copay. MRI, CT or PET scan: $50 copay. Out of network: plan pays 70%. Whether an MRI needs prior authorization is not stated; check Aetna's online precertification list.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: Is birth control covered?
Answer: Yes. Student Health offers gynecologic and sexual health care; reproductive health needs no referral. Generic and over-the-counter birth control is $0 at in-network pharmacies, up to a 12-month supply; brand-name methods are $0 when no generic exists. Contraceptive counseling is covered at 100% (2 visits per year).

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: Is therapy covered, and for how many sessions?
Answer: Counseling at Student Health is covered by the Clinical Fee. Outside therapy needs no referral: $10 copay per visit in network, no deductible, telemedicine included. No session limit is listed. Out of network: plan pays 70%.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: What is my deductible?
Answer: $400 in network (with a referral) and $1,500 out of network (including care without a referral), per person per year. Many services skip the deductible, including preventive care, the ER, prescriptions, mental health and vision.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: What's the most I could pay in a year?
Answer: The out-of-pocket maximum is $1,500 per person ($3,000 per family) in network, and $4,000 per person ($8,000 per family) out of network. The two totals are counted separately.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Costs
text:
Question: What happens if I go to an out-of-network doctor?
Answer: The plan pays 70% after the $1,500 out-of-network deductible, with a $4,000 out-of-pocket maximum. The doctor may bill you the difference (balance billing), except where the No Surprises Act protects you; in emergencies you only owe your normal share.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Booking
text:
Question: How do I make an appointment at Student Health?
Answer: Call 215-746-WELL (9355). After your first visit you can book online in PennChart.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Booking
text:
Question: What are Student Health's hours during breaks and summer?
Answer: Normal hours: Mon–Wed 9 am–7:30 pm; Thu 10 am–6 pm; Fri 9 am–5 pm; Sat 10 am–3 pm; Sun closed. Break hours are posted in an alert bar on the Wellness site. Phone line is 24/7.

heading_path: Curated answers > Before care > Booking
text:
Question: How do I book a first appointment at CAPS?
Answer: CAPS is now Counseling at Student Health and Counseling. Call 215-746-WELL (9355) any time or drop in at 3624 Market St.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the visit
text:
Question: What should I bring to my appointment?
Answer: Your Aetna insurance card (printed or in the Aetna Health app), a photo ID, your list of medicines and allergies, and your referral details if seeing an outside provider.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the visit
text:
Question: Where do I find my insurance card and member ID?
Answer: Print it from the Aetna Student Health website, or open it in the Aetna Health app.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the visit
text:
Question: The clinic asked if I have insurance. What do I tell them?
Answer: "I have Aetna Student Health through the Penn Student Insurance Plan," and show the card. Mention your Student Health referral if you have one.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the visit
text:
Question: The clinic wants me to pay upfront. Is that normal?
Answer: In-network clinics often collect the copay at the visit; the rest is billed after Aetna processes the claim. Aetna does not pay out-of-network providers directly, so they may ask you to pay in full. Keep the itemized receipt and send Aetna a claim form within 90 days.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the visit
text:
Question: The doctor wants to send my test to an outside lab. Will I be charged?
Answer: Possibly. The lab bills your insurance: a $35 copay if the lab is in Aetna's network, more if it is not (plan pays 70% after the deductible). Ask which lab it is and check it is in Aetna's network.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: Is my medication covered?
Answer: Look the drug up in the 2026 Aetna Pharmacy Drug Guide (Advanced Control Plan, Aetna Student Health PA). Each drug has a tier: PG preferred generic ($20), PB preferred brand ($50), NP non-preferred ($75), PSP or NPSP specialty, and NF not covered unless an exception is granted. Codes show limits: PA prior authorization, QL quantity limit, ST step therapy. Brand names are in capitals, generics in lowercase. The list can change during the year, so confirm on the Aetna member website or at 800-841-5374.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: How much will my prescription cost?
Answer: Depends on the drug tier. For a 30-day supply: preferred generic $20, preferred brand $50, non-preferred generic or brand $75; no deductible. Insulin is capped at $25 per 30 days. Many birth control methods cost $0. If you ask for a brand when a generic exists, you also pay the price difference.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: Which pharmacy should I use?
Answer: Any pharmacy in Aetna's network (more than 68,000, including CVS near campus). At an out-of-network pharmacy you pay full price and must file a claim.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: The pharmacy says my drug needs prior authorization. What does that mean?
Answer: Aetna must approve the drug before it pays. Your doctor sends the request, usually online. Contact the doctor who prescribed it.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: The pharmacy says my drug isn't covered. What can I do?
Answer: Ask your doctor for a covered alternative or a generic, or to request an exception. For a denial, contact the Insurance Navigators (215-746-4200).

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: Can I get a generic version to pay less?
Answer: Usually yes. Generics have the same active ingredients and meet the same FDA standards. Ask your doctor or pharmacist.

heading_path: Curated answers > During care > At the pharmacy
text:
Question: How do I refill my prescription?
Answer: Ask your pharmacy for a refill, or order through the Aetna member website. For drugs you take regularly, CVS Caremark Mail Service Pharmacy can mail up to a 90-day supply; order online or call 1-888-792-3862. Standard shipping is free.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Understanding documents
text:
Question: What is an EOB?
Answer: An Explanation of Benefits is Aetna's statement of what the provider charged, what Aetna paid and what you may owe. It is not a bill.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Understanding documents
text:
Question: What do the fields on my EOB mean?
Answer: Provider and date; amount billed (full charge); allowed amount (most Aetna pays); plan paid; patient responsibility (split into deductible, copay, coinsurance); remark codes explaining denials.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Understanding documents
text:
Question: What does "patient responsibility" mean?
Answer: What you may owe after Aetna pays. Wait for the provider's bill and compare.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Understanding documents
text:
Question: What does "applied to deductible" mean?
Answer: That amount counts toward your yearly deductible, so you pay it.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Understanding documents
text:
Question: What's the difference between an EOB and a bill?
Answer: The EOB comes from Aetna and explains the claim. The bill comes from the provider and asks for payment.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Understanding documents
text:
Question: Why does my EOB say "this is not a bill"?
Answer: Aetna is only reporting how it processed the claim. Pay only when the provider sends a bill.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Common surprise bills
text:
Question: Why was I charged for lab work done at Student Health?
Answer: The sample was taken at Student Health but tested by an outside lab, which billed your insurance. Your share is a $35 copay at an in-network lab, more at an out-of-network lab.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Common surprise bills
text:
Question: Why did I get a bill from a doctor I never met?
Answer: Hospitals often send separate bills for the building and for each doctor, such as a radiologist. The No Surprises Act limits out-of-network charges in emergencies and at in-network hospitals.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Common surprise bills
text:
Question: Why is my bill from Penn Medicine and not Aetna?
Answer: Providers send bills; Aetna does not. Penn Medicine bills you after Aetna processes the claim. Penn Medicine billing: 800-406-1177.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Contacts
text:
Question: Who do I contact about a bill?
Answer: Start with the Insurance Navigators (215-746-4200, wel-shsinsur@pobox.upenn.edu). Claim questions: Aetna, 800-841-5374. Penn Medicine payment: 800-406-1177.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Contacts
text:
Question: When should I contact the Insurance Navigators?
Answer: When a bill or EOB is confusing, a referral may have been missed, a claim was denied, or you don't know who to call. Office: 3535 Market St, Suite 60.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Contacts
text:
Question: When should I call Aetna?
Answer: For claim status, what was paid, ID cards, adding dependents and finding in-network doctors: 800-841-5374.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Contacts
text:
Question: When should I call the clinic's billing office?
Answer: To get an itemized bill, set up a payment plan, or check the claim was sent to Aetna correctly.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Contacts
text:
Question: Can someone help me read my bill?
Answer: Yes: the Insurance Navigators, and Aetna's Personal Navigators through 800-841-5374.

heading_path: Curated answers > After care > Contacts
text:
Question: I can't afford this bill. Is there help?
Answer: Ask the provider for a payment plan. For Penn Medicine bills, apply for financial assistance at 800-406-1177 or in MyChart; interpreters are available. Also contact the Insurance Navigators.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Away from Philadelphia
text:
Question: I'm sick while traveling in another US city. What do I do?
Answer: Use any Aetna in-network provider (find one in the Aetna Health app). No referral needed more than 25 miles from campus. Emergency: nearest ER.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Away from Philadelphia
text:
Question: Does PSIP cover me over the summer?
Answer: Yes, with annual coverage: August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027. Spring-only coverage runs January 1 to July 31, 2027.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Away from Philadelphia
text:
Question: I'm going home to China. Am I covered there?
Answer: Yes. Care received outside the United States is paid at the in-network level; submit the claim with the provider's medical and payment details. On Call International helps with referrals and emergencies abroad (1-603-328-1956 collect).

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Away from Philadelphia
text:
Question: I got care abroad. How do I get reimbursed?
Answer: Keep itemized bills and receipts, then file a claim form with Aetna (800-841-5374). Give Aetna written notice within 20 days and send the completed claim within 90 days of the care, or as soon as reasonably possible.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Away from Philadelphia
text:
Question: I'm on an internship in another state. How do I use my insurance?
Answer: Use Aetna in-network providers there; no referral is needed beyond 25 miles.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Away from Philadelphia
text:
Question: How do I get enough medication before going home?
Answer: Ask your doctor and pharmacy for a larger supply. In-network retail or mail order pharmacies can fill up to a 90-day supply ($60, $150 or $225 copay by tier); out-of-network pharmacies cannot fill more than 30 days. Birth control: up to 12 months. Lost or stolen prescriptions are not replaced.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Life changes
text:
Question: I'm graduating. When does my coverage end?
Answer: Coverage runs to the end of the period you enrolled for, normally July 31. December graduates not returning in the spring: coverage ends January 31, 2027, and enrolled dependents' coverage ends with it.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Life changes
text:
Question: What happens to my insurance if I take a leave of absence?
Answer: You can buy PSIP by asking the Insurance Navigators for an LOA Insurance application (215-746-WELL or wel-shsinsur@pobox.upenn.edu). No referrals needed while on leave.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Life changes
text:
Question: Can my spouse or child use PSIP?
Answer: Yes, if you are enrolled first. Spouse or domestic partner (with a Penn Guest Card) and unmarried children under 26 who live with you. $5,018 per year each; $10,036 for two or more children; paid to Aetna. Newborns are covered 31 days and must be enrolled in that time.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Life changes
text:
Question: My parents are visiting and one got sick. Are they covered?
Answer: No. Only enrolled students and enrolled spouses, partners and children are covered. Parents need their own travel insurance.

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Extra benefits
text:
Question: Does PSIP include vision or dental?
Answer: Limited. Eye exam: plan pays 90% in network, 1 per year, no referral; glasses or contacts up to $125 per year. Dental: only impacted wisdom teeth and injury to natural teeth, paid at 90%. Optional plans: Aetna Vision Preferred ($65 per year), Penn Student Dental Plan, Aetna Student Dental Plan ($395 per year).

heading_path: Curated answers > Special situations > Extra benefits
text:
Question: What is the Vital Savings program?
Answer: An optional Aetna dental discount program. It is not insurance, and Penn Dental Family Practice does not accept it.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What does "deductible" mean?
Answer: What you pay each year for covered care before insurance starts sharing costs. PSIP: $400 in network (with a referral) and $1,500 out of network (including care without a referral).

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What's the difference between a copay and coinsurance?
Answer: A copay is a fixed amount per service (for example $30). Coinsurance is a percentage of the cost (for example 20%), usually after the deductible.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What is an "out-of-pocket maximum"?
Answer: The most you pay in a year for covered care; after that the plan pays 100%. Premiums don't count. PSIP: $1,500 per person in network, $4,000 out of network.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What do "in network" and "out of network" mean?
Answer: In network: providers with an Aetna contract, so you pay less. Out of network: no contract, so you pay more and may be balance billed.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What is "prior authorization"?
Answer: Approval from Aetna before certain services or drugs are covered. Your doctor asks for it.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What is a "referral"?
Answer: Written approval from your main doctor to see a specialist. For PSIP it comes from Student Health and lasts until July 31.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What does "allowed amount" mean on my EOB?
Answer: The most Aetna will pay a provider for a service.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What do "claim," "denial" and "appeal" mean?
Answer: Claim: a request to Aetna to pay for care. Denial: Aetna refusing to pay. Appeal: asking Aetna to reconsider a denial (get help from the Insurance Navigators).

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What is a "premium"?
Answer: What you pay to have insurance, even if you don't use care. PSIP: $5,018 for 2026–27.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What are a "formulary" and "drug tiers"?
Answer: The formulary is the list of covered drugs. Tiers are cost levels; higher tiers cost more.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What does "balance billing" mean?
Answer: When an out-of-network provider bills you the difference between its price and what Aetna allows. Limited by the No Surprises Act in emergencies.

heading_path: Curated answers > Insurance terms > Insurance terms
text:
Question: What does "PPO" mean?
Answer: Preferred Provider Organization: you can see in- or out-of-network providers, but in network costs less. PSIP is an Aetna PPO plus a Student Health referral rule.
